# Roadmap {#sec-roadmap .unnumbered}

This page says where the book is going. The first chapter is written and the second has begun. Everything after that is a plan, and the
plan changes as the experiments come in: stages have already been moved, merged and left out, and that will
happen again.

The order follows the five breakthroughs of *A Brief History of Intelligence*. Each is one chapter, each belongs
to a group of animals, and each builds on the brain of the chapter before it.

| chapter | animals | what the brain gains | |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Steering | the first worms | good and bad, needs, moods, a first kind of learning, telling look-alikes apart | written |
| 2. Reinforcing | the first fish | learning from reward what to do | in progress |
| 3. Simulating | the first mammals | trying something in the head before doing it | planned |
| 4. Mentalizing | primates | a model of its own mind, and of the minds of others | planned |
| 5. Speaking | humans | knowledge that passes from one brain to another | far off |

## Chapter 1: steering

The brain of a small worm. It turns what it sees into movement (@sec-steering), sorts the world into good and bad
(@sec-valence), stops reacting to what is always there (@sec-habituation), learns in one life which new foods
hurt (@sec-association), looks after hunger and cold (@sec-drives), and stays in a state for a while after a meal
or a poison bite, a state that builds up over several bites (@sec-affect). Last, a region with random wiring
spreads the look of a thing out over many cells, so that things that look alike can still be told apart, even when
only a combination of features says which is which (@sec-pallium). Insects have such a region, the mushroom body;
in vertebrates it is the oldest part of the pallium.

This creature learns one thing: what to stay away from, taught by pain. It cannot learn what is worth going to, it
cannot unlearn, and it cannot learn what to do.

## Chapter 2: reinforcing

The brain of an early fish. The first vertebrates hunted in open water, and nearly all the parts of the vertebrate
brain were already there. What they add is learning from *surprise*: the difference between what happened and
what was expected. This chapter adds the parts in the following order.

- **Dopamine** (@sec-critic). A cell that fires when things turn out better than expected, and falls silent
  when they turn out worse. With it the creature learns what predicts food, and what predicts the thing that
  predicts food. It also learns to like, and to unlearn, which chapter 1 could not do.
- **Hands.** Until here the creature eats what it grasps. Now it can pick something up, hold it and eat it later,
  so that there is something to choose between.
- **The basal ganglia.** The same dopamine signal teaches which *action* to take. This is learning by trial and
  error, as in a rat that learns to press a lever.
- **Curiosity.** New things become a little rewarding in themselves, so that the creature tries what it does not
  know yet.
- **The hippocampus.** A map of places, made from the creature's sense of its own movement and from landmarks, so
  that it can learn where food is, not only what it looks like, and go back there when it is out of sight. It
  comes after the basal ganglia: a map is of use only to a creature that can learn which way to turn at a place.
  Goldfish without this part of the pallium can still learn to swim to a marker, but no longer to a place.

Parked until these work: precise timing (the cerebellum), and modulators that set how fast the creature learns when
its world is steady or changing.

Two things change in how the stages are done. The circuits are designed and tested before any evolution, and
evolution then tunes them, in fewer generations than in chapter 1. And the learning stages get *lab experiments*:
one creature in a scripted situation, as in an animal lab, to see whether it learns the way real animals do.

## Chapter 3: simulating

The brain of an early mammal, and its new part, the neocortex. The cortex learns to predict what the creature will
sense next. Once it can do that, it can be run without the world: the creature stops at a choice, plays out each
option, and picks the one that ends best.

The planned stages: a cortex that predicts, trying actions in the head at a choice point, routes stored on the
map of chapter 2 and replayed during rest and sleep, holding a goal through distractions, and remembering a single event.

The tests are the classic ones from the rat lab. An animal that explored a maze without reward goes straight to
food that appears there later. An animal whose path is blocked takes a detour. An animal that has had enough of
one food stops working for it at once.

## Chapter 4: mentalizing

The brain of a primate, living in a group in which the others matter. The brain first gets a model of itself:
what it knows, and how sure it is. Applied to another creature, the same model says what that creature wants and what
it has seen.

The planned stages: knowing when it does not know, reading the goals of others, learning a skill by watching, and
preparing for a need it does not feel yet, such as storing food before the winter.

## Chapter 5: speaking

The human step. Calls with a fixed meaning come first, then signals whose meaning is agreed on within a group,
then naming what two creatures are both looking at. The aim at the end is knowledge that no single life could find
again and that still grows from one generation to the next.

This chapter is the least certain, both in what is known about evolution and in whether a small grid world can
carry it.

## The world grows too

A brain can only be tested on what its world asks of it, so the world grows with the brain. It takes more and
more of the rules of *One Hour One Life*: tools, fire and cooking, and chains of steps that are too long to find
by accident. Animals that move by themselves come in as prey and as predators.

For the last two chapters, the way lives are run has to change as well. A generation now starts and ends
together. Creatures that watch, imitate and teach each other need parents, children and lives that overlap.
